::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The short version
- **Finish line:** you can explain the Common Rule, the program's single-IRB waiver, HIPAA's research
  pathways and Certificates of Confidentiality well enough to know what the privacy officer and the
  IRB must confirm before EXT-21 runs on real data, and what a Certificate means for IT.
- **Punchline:** the medical director says "the IRB waived consent, so we're covered." The privacy
  officer says that settles one question, and HIPAA is a different one. Her written determination:
  Lakeshore discloses a **limited data set under a data use agreement**, keeps the donor-key
  crosswalk at home, and, with counsel, **treats EXT-21 output and the crosswalk as covered by a
  Certificate of Confidentiality** as a conservative organizational decision.
- **The rule in one line:** three layers, three owners. The Common Rule is the program's IRB
  pathway, HIPAA is Lakeshore's own legal basis for disclosing, and the Certificate limits what
  anyone may do with the data afterwards, "for perpetuity."
- **Monday question:** "Show me every place a copy of EXT-21 output or the crosswalk exists today,
  including backups and test copies, and who gets the call if a subpoena names them."
- **The trap:** treating a Certificate as a shield for BECS or as a reason to stop thinking about
  HIPAA. It is neither. It is an extra restriction on research data, and it makes your copy
  inventory a legal matter.
:::

## "The IRB waived consent, so we're fine"

The privacy officer has asked for a meeting about RSH-0107, Lakeshore's internal research
participation file. Around the table: the privacy officer, counsel (in-house, there to listen and
advise), the medical director, you, and your Quality Analyst. The hub has sent the program's
human-subjects paperwork: a note that a single IRB (institutional review board) has granted a
waiver of informed consent for the program's blood donors.

The medical director is relieved. "That's the hard part done. The ethics board looked at it and
waived consent. We can start the monthly feed."

The privacy officer doesn't raise her voice. "That's the Common Rule question, and it's answered for
the program. It isn't my question. My question is what *Lakeshore's* legal basis is for handing
donor information to someone outside the building. Those are different rules with different owners."

Counsel adds a second wrinkle. "And since the research is federally funded, there's a third thing
to decide. Whether any of what we send, or any copy we keep, carries a Certificate of
Confidentiality. If it does, a subpoena doesn't work the way people expect."

Your Quality Analyst asks: "If it's covered by a Certificate, can FDA still inspect our BECS
records?" Nobody answers right away.

You open RSH-0107 and write three headings: **Common Rule, HIPAA, Certificate.** The rest of this
lesson fills them in.

## Why these rules exist, and the ITSM bridge

Each layer prevents a different failure.

- **Human-subjects rules** exist because research on people has gone wrong in ways the people
  never agreed to. They put an independent reviewer (the IRB) between a research idea and the
  people it uses. The failure prevented: a study that nobody independent asked "is this fair to
  the people in it?"
- **HIPAA** exists because health information moves between organizations. It says when a covered
  entity may let it go. The failure prevented: a health organization disclosing identifiable
  information because someone senior said yes.
- **Certificates of Confidentiality** exist because a research subject who gives information to a
  study can have it pulled out by a court order, a subpoena or an agency request. The failure
  prevented: research participants being harmed, or refusing to take part, because their study
  data can be compelled.

The ITSM bridge is **information security management plus change enablement with a legal
dimension**. You already classify data and keep a CMDB (configuration management database). The new
idea is that the classification comes from three separate legal determinations, and each changes
what your service desk, backup team and decommissioning process may do. The discipline is knowing
which determination put the label there, and who can change it.

Lakeshore is treated as a HIPAA covered entity for this curriculum. That was settled in
[Information governance in a covered entity](../../healthcare-security-and-privacy/information-governance-in-a-covered-entity/index.qmd),
and this lesson doesn't reopen it. For the baseline Privacy Rule ideas (permitted uses,
authorizations, minimum necessary), read
[The HIPAA Privacy Rule](../../healthcare-security-and-privacy/the-hipaa-privacy-rule/index.qmd)
first. This lesson takes the research-specific provisions that module left aside.

## The rule in plain English

**Layer 1, the Common Rule (45 CFR Part 46, Subpart A).** Federal rules protect people in research.
Research that involves identifiable private information about a living person is "human subjects
research." An IRB must approve it against a set of criteria, one of which is privacy and
confidentiality. Consent is the default, and an IRB may waive it only on findings it must document.
The program says one single IRB did that for the program's donors and patients. That is the
program's pathway.

**Layer 2, HIPAA's research pathways (45 CFR 164.512(i) and 164.514(e)).** A covered entity needs a
basis to disclose protected health information (PHI). For research, the Privacy Rule offers
several. In 164.512(i), an IRB or privacy board can approve a waiver of the individual's
authorization (and the covered entity must receive documentation of it), or a researcher can give
specified representations for a preparatory review or for research on decedents. In 164.514(e), a
covered entity can disclose a **limited data set** (PHI with a list of direct identifiers removed)
under a **data use agreement**. The covered entity chooses. Lakeshore's privacy officer chooses the
limited data set.

**Layer 3, the Certificate of Confidentiality (42 U.S.C. 241(d), NIH policy NOT-OD-17-109).**
Federal law says identifiable, sensitive research information is protected: it can't be disclosed
to people not connected with the research, except in four named situations, and it is immune from
legal process. For NIH-funded research within its scope, NIH's policy says a Certificate is issued
automatically. The protection lasts "for perpetuity" and follows copies.

Whether, and how far, that third layer reaches *Lakeshore* is where this lesson is careful. The
statute and policy are written for people "engaged in" research and for NIH award recipients. They
do not say, in the text we hold, what happens to a contributing blood center's own copies. So
Lakeshore doesn't claim the statute settles it. It makes a documented organizational decision to
behave as if it did.

## The actual text

### Common Rule: what counts as research and as a human subject

**45 CFR 46.102(l), opening sentence:**

> (l) *Research* means a systematic investigation, including research development, testing, and
> evaluation, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge.

*In our scenario.* A monthly feed into a database built to study the transfusion chain is designed to
contribute to generalizable knowledge. That is why the program runs under an IRB. Lakeshore reviewing
its own deferral coding to run operations is a different thing.

**45 CFR 46.102(e)(1)(ii), 46.102(e)(4) and 46.102(e)(5):**

> (e)(1) *Human subject* means a living individual about whom an investigator (whether professional
> or student) conducting research: [...] (ii) Obtains, uses, studies, analyzes, or generates
> identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens.

> (4) *Private information* includes information about behavior that occurs in a context in which an
> individual can reasonably expect that no observation or recording is taking place, and
> information that has been provided for specific purposes by an individual and that the
> individual can reasonably expect will not be made public (*e.g.,* a medical record).

> (5) *Identifiable private information* is private information for which the identity of the
> subject is or may readily be ascertained by the investigator or associated with the information.

*In our scenario.* A donor gives information to a blood center for a specific purpose and expects
it not to be made public, so donor records fit "private information." The question is the next
step: is the identity of the subject "or may readily be ascertained by the investigator or
associated with the information"? Lakeshore's extract carries a random code, and Lakeshore alone
holds the crosswalk. Whether coded information counts as identifiable *for the investigator* is
exactly the kind of judgment the IRB makes. The local excerpt doesn't include any guidance on
coded information, so this lesson doesn't decide it. What the privacy officer needs to see is
that the IRB considered it, and in what words.

One more clause matters to IT. 46.102(e)(7) tells federal departments to "reexamine the meaning" of
identifiable private information regularly (at least every 4 years). The line between identifiable
and not is expected to move as re-identification techniques improve.

**45 CFR 46.101(a), what the policy applies to:**

> (a) Except as detailed in § 46.104, this policy applies to all research involving human subjects
> conducted, supported, or otherwise subject to regulation by any Federal department or agency that
> takes appropriate administrative action to make the policy applicable to such research.

*In our scenario.* The program is supported by NHLBI. Which entities are bound directly, and which
through the hub's agreement, is a question the agreement answers (see row 8 below).

### Common Rule: what an IRB must find, and how consent is waived

**45 CFR 46.111(a)(7):**

> (7) When appropriate, there are adequate provisions to protect the privacy of subjects and to
> maintain the confidentiality of data.

That is one of the criteria the IRB "shall determine" are satisfied before approving research
(46.111(a)). Others are that risks are minimized and reasonable, that subject selection is
equitable, and that consent is sought or waived "in accordance with" 46.116 and 46.117.

*In our scenario.* The IRB's privacy finding is about the research plan. It is not an inspection of
Lakeshore's network. The privacy officer still decides what Lakeshore sends and how.

**45 CFR 46.116(f)(3), the waiver criteria, as written:**

> (3) *Requirements for waiver and alteration.* In order for an IRB to waive or alter consent as
> described in this subsection, the IRB must find and document that:
>
> (i) The research involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;
>
> (ii) The research could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration;
>
> (iii) If the research involves using identifiable private information or identifiable
> biospecimens, the research could not practicably be carried out without using such information
> or biospecimens in an identifiable format;
>
> (iv) The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects; and
>
> (v) Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided
> with additional pertinent information after participation.

*In our scenario.* Condition (iii) is the IRB's finding about the *research*. It doesn't mean
Lakeshore must send identifiers. The privacy officer separately asks whether identifiers are needed
at all, and here they are not.

**The program's statement.** The 2022 design paper says, in its own words: "A waiver of informed
consent was requested and granted by the single IRB for both hospital patients and blood donors."
It is a statement in a peer-reviewed paper about the earlier phase. It is the paper, not an IRB
approval letter, and it's about consent under the Common Rule. Note what it doesn't say. It doesn't
say a HIPAA authorization was waived, and it doesn't tell us which IRB, what date or which
protocol covers the current round. Those are what Lakeshore asks the hub for.

### HIPAA: the research pathways in 164.512(i)

**45 CFR 164.512(i)(1), opening and the first pathway:**

> (i) *Standard: Uses and disclosures for research purposes*—(1) *Permitted uses and
> disclosures.* A covered entity may use or disclose protected health information for research,
> regardless of the source of funding of the research, provided that:
>
> (i) *Board approval of a waiver of authorization.* The covered entity obtains documentation that
> an alteration to or waiver, in whole or in part, of the individual authorization required by
> § 164.508 for use or disclosure of protected health information has been approved by either:
>
> (A) An Institutional Review Board (IRB), [...] or
>
> (B) A privacy board that: (*1*) Has members with varying backgrounds and appropriate professional
> competency [...]; (*2*) Includes at least one member who is not affiliated with the covered entity,
> not affiliated with any entity conducting or sponsoring the research, and not related to any
> person who is affiliated with any of such entities; and (*3*) Does not have any member
> participating in a review of any project in which the member has a conflict of interest.

*Reading it.* The covered entity must "obtain documentation" of an authorization waiver. A Common Rule
consent waiver and a HIPAA authorization waiver are different findings under different rules, even
when one board grants both.

**164.512(i)(2), what the documentation must contain.** The IRB or board's identity and date, a
statement that the waiver criteria are met, a brief description of the PHI needed, the review
procedure used and the chair's signature. The criteria include "no more than a minimal risk to the
privacy of individuals," based on at least an adequate plan to protect identifiers, an adequate plan
to destroy them "at the earliest opportunity consistent with conduct of the research," and written
assurances against reuse or further disclosure, plus findings that the research "could not
practicably be conducted" without the waiver or without the PHI.

*The other two pathways.* Section 164.512(i)(1)(ii) allows **reviews preparatory to research**, with
the researcher's representations that PHI is sought "solely to review protected health
information as necessary to prepare a research protocol," that none is removed from the covered
entity, and that it is necessary. Section 164.512(i)(1)(iii) allows **research on decedents**, with
the researcher's representation, documentation of death on request, and a necessity
representation. Neither fits a recurring extract of living donors' data leaving Lakeshore.

### HIPAA: the limited data set in 164.514(e)

**164.514(e)(1) and (e)(2):**

> (e)(1) *Standard: Limited data set.* A covered entity may use or disclose a limited data set that
> meets the requirements of paragraphs (e)(2) and (e)(3) of this section, if the covered entity
> enters into a data use agreement with the limited data set recipient, in accordance with
> paragraph (e)(4) of this section.
>
> (2) *Implementation specification: Limited data set:* A limited data set is protected health
> information that excludes the following direct identifiers of the individual or of relatives,
> employers, or household members of the individual: (i) Names; (ii) Postal address information,
> other than town or city, State, and zip code; (iii) Telephone numbers; (iv) Fax numbers; (v)
> Electronic mail addresses; (vi) Social security numbers; (vii) Medical record numbers; (viii)
> Health plan beneficiary numbers; (ix) Account numbers; (x) Certificate/license numbers; (xi)
> Vehicle identifiers and serial numbers, including license plate numbers; (xii) Device
> identifiers and serial numbers; (xiii) Web Universal Resource Locators (URLs); (xiv) Internet
> Protocol (IP) address numbers; (xv) Biometric identifiers, including finger and voice prints; and
> (xvi) Full face photographic images and any comparable images.

*In our scenario.* Three observations. First, a limited data set **is still PHI**, so Lakeshore's
HIPAA obligations (security, incident response, minimum necessary habits) stay in force. Second,
**dates are not on the list.** Donation dates, collection and manufacturing timing, and the
sequence of a donor's visits can stay. Third, town or city, State and zip code can stay. The
program needs dates, because a vein-to-vein study is about timing, so that is what makes this the
natural pathway. Whether a number such as a donation identification number or donor number counts as
one of the listed identifiers (a "medical record number" or "account number," for instance) is a
call the privacy officer makes field by field. The regulation lists categories, not Lakeshore's field
names.

**164.514(e)(3), purposes:**

> (3)(i) A covered entity may use or disclose a limited data set under paragraph (e)(1) of this
> section only for the purposes of research, public health, or health care operations.
>
> (ii) A covered entity may use protected health information to create a limited data set that
> meets the requirements of paragraph (e)(2) of this section, or disclose protected health
> information only to a business associate for such purpose, whether or not the limited data set is
> to be used by the covered entity.

*In our scenario.* The disclosure is for research, so it's in bounds. And (e)(3)(ii) is what lets
Lakeshore's own workforce, running EXT-21, create the limited data set from PHI in BECS.

**164.514(e)(4), the data use agreement.** The agreement must provide satisfactory assurance "that
the limited data set recipient will only use or disclose the protected health information for
limited purposes." Its contents:

> (ii) *Contents.* A data use agreement between the covered entity and the limited data set
> recipient must:
>
> (A) Establish the permitted uses and disclosures of such information by the limited data set
> recipient, consistent with paragraph (e)(3) of this section. The data use agreement may not
> authorize the limited data set recipient to use or further disclose the information in a manner
> that would violate the requirements of this subpart, if done by the covered entity;
>
> (B) Establish who is permitted to use or receive the limited data set; and
>
> (C) Provide that the limited data set recipient will:
>
> (*1*) Not use or further disclose the information other than as permitted by the data use
> agreement or as otherwise required by law;
>
> (*2*) Use appropriate safeguards to prevent use or disclosure of the information other than as
> provided for by the data use agreement;
>
> (*3*) Report to the covered entity any use or disclosure of the information not provided for by
> its data use agreement of which it becomes aware;
>
> (*4*) Ensure that any agents to whom it provides the limited data set agree to the same
> restrictions and conditions that apply to the limited data set recipient with respect to such
> information; and
>
> (*5*) Not identify the information or contact the individuals.

*In our scenario.* Read these as a checklist for the document, and as a map of what IT will later
be asked to prove. Clause (B), "who is permitted to use or receive," forces a question module 1
left open: **which entities will actually hold Lakeshore's data?** The hub, the Data Coordinating
Center, the lab center? Clause (C)(4) pulls any agents into the same terms. Clause (C)(5), "not
identify the information or contact the individuals," is why the crosswalk never leaves
Lakeshore: the recipient has no key, and the agreement forbids trying to build one.

**164.514(e)(4)(iii), the covered entity's own exposure:**

> (iii) *Compliance.* (A) A covered entity is not in compliance with the standards in paragraph (e)
> of this section if the covered entity knew of a pattern of activity or practice of the limited
> data set recipient that constituted a material breach or violation of the data use agreement,
> unless the covered entity took reasonable steps to cure the breach or end the violation, as
> applicable, and, if such steps were unsuccessful: (1) Discontinued disclosure of protected health
> information to the recipient; and (2) Reported the problem to the Secretary.

*In our scenario.* Lakeshore can't sign the agreement and forget it. If it learns of a pattern of
violations, it has to act, and one of the available actions is to stop sending. IT's part is a
transfer that can actually be paused, and a log showing what was sent when.

Notice what the text does **not** contain. It lists no required terms about how long the recipient
keeps the data, or returning or destroying it at the end. Those would be Lakeshore's to negotiate
into the agreement. The paper says the program retains source data "allowing for potential new
analyses," so that conversation is real, and module 4 takes it up.

### The de-identification question we are not answering

HIPAA has a separate de-identification route in 164.514(a) and (b). This course's local sources don't
include that text, so we don't quote or apply it. We note one thing: a **coded** data set is not
automatically "de-identified." That is part of why the privacy officer chose the limited data set,
which has its own written terms.

### Certificates of Confidentiality: the statute

**42 U.S.C. 241(d)(1)(A)(i):**

> (A) If a person is engaged in biomedical, behavioral, clinical, or other research, in which
> identifiable, sensitive information is collected [...] the Secretary, in coordination with other
> agencies, as applicable— (i) shall issue to such person a certificate of confidentiality to
> protect the privacy of individuals who are the subjects of such research if the research is
> funded wholly or in part by the Federal Government;

**The disclosure prohibition, 241(d)(1)(B), and its exceptions in (C):**

> (B) Except as provided in subparagraph (C), any person to whom a certificate is issued under
> subparagraph (A) [...] shall not disclose or provide to any other person not connected with the
> research the name of such an individual or any information, document, or biospecimen that
> contains identifiable, sensitive information about such an individual and that was created or
> compiled for purposes of the research.
>
> (C) The disclosure prohibition in subparagraph (B) shall not apply to disclosure or use that is—
> (i) required by Federal, State, or local laws, excluding instances described in subparagraph (D);
> (ii) necessary for the medical treatment of the individual to whom the information, document, or
> biospecimen pertains and made with the consent of such individual; (iii) made with the consent of
> the individual to whom the information, document, or biospecimen pertains; or (iv) made for the
> purposes of other scientific research that is in compliance with applicable Federal regulations
> governing the protection of human subjects in research.

**Legal process and "perpetuity," 241(d)(1)(D) to (F):**

> (D) Any person to whom a certificate is issued [...] shall not, in any Federal, State, or local
> civil, criminal, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding, disclose or provide the name of
> such individual or any such information, document, or biospecimen that contains identifiable,
> sensitive information about the individual and that was created or compiled for purposes of the
> research, except in the circumstance described in subparagraph (C)(iii).
>
> (E) Identifiable, sensitive information protected under subparagraph (A), and all copies
> thereof, shall be immune from the legal process, and shall not, without the consent of the
> individual to whom the information pertains, be admissible as evidence or used for any purpose in
> any action, suit, or other judicial, legislative, or administrative proceeding.
>
> (F) Identifiable, sensitive information collected by a person to whom a certificate has been
> issued under subparagraph (A), and all copies thereof, shall be subject to the protections
> afforded by this section for perpetuity.

**The definition, 241(d)(4):**

> (4) For purposes of this subsection, the term "identifiable, sensitive information" means
> information that is about an individual and that is gathered or used during the course of
> research described in paragraph (1)(A) and— (A) through which an individual is identified; or
> (B) for which there is at least a very small risk, as determined by current scientific practices
> or statistical methods, that some combination of the information, a request for the information,
> and other available data sources could be used to deduce the identity of an individual.

*In our scenario.* Four points matter to IT.

1. **"All copies thereof."** Immunity and perpetuity attach to copies, not to the original file. Your
   backup tape is a copy. So is the file on the staging server and the test copy.
2. **The definition reaches past direct identifiers.** Clause (B), "at least a very small risk," is
   a much lower bar than "someone can read the donor's name." Dates, town and zip code, and rare
   component attributes can together point to a person with enough outside data. So the removal of
   direct identifiers in a limited data set doesn't take the data out of a Certificate's definition.
3. **The exceptions are narrow.** Legal requirements are an exception, but not in a "civil, criminal,
   administrative, legislative, or other proceeding." Consent is an exception. Other compliant
   scientific research is an exception. A subpoena is not on the list.
4. **"Created or compiled for purposes of the research."** The wording speaks of research
   information. BECS records exist for blood operations and for FDA's recordkeeping rules. Nothing
   in the text we hold makes a Certificate a bar on the FDA obligations attached to BECS. This is a
   reading for counsel to confirm, but it is the reason Quality can stop worrying about the
   inspection question while counsel does the confirming.

### Certificates of Confidentiality: NIH's policy

NOT-OD-17-109 is how NIH implements the statute for NIH-funded research. Three passages carry the
weight for this lesson.

**Scope.** The policy "applies to all biomedical, behavioral, clinical, or other research funded
wholly or in part by the NIH, whether supported through grants, cooperative agreements, contracts,
other transaction awards, or conducted by the NIH Intramural Research Program, that collects or
uses identifiable, sensitive information."

**Automatic issuance.** Research "within the scope of this Policy is deemed to be issued a
Certificate through this Policy and is therefore required to protect the privacy of individuals who
are subjects of such research in accordance with subsection 301(d) of the Public Health Service Act."
It adds that "Institutions and their investigators are responsible for determining whether research
they conduct is subject to this Policy and therefore issued a Certificate. Certificates issued in
this manner will not be issued as a separate document."

**Copies and non-NIH-funded recipients.** "Recipients of Certificates are required to ensure that any
investigator or institution not funded by NIH who receives a copy of identifiable, sensitive
information protected by a Certificate issued by this Policy, understand they are also subject to the
requirements of subsection 301(d) of the Public Health Service Act."

*In our scenario.* The program's contracts are NIH-funded (module 1, from NIH RePORTER), so the
program's own research appears to be inside the policy's scope. Notice what this passage describes:
the Certificate holder passes responsibilities on to non-NIH-funded institutions that **receive a
copy**. That is the direction of flow from the program *outward*. Lakeshore sits on the other side:
it is the source of the data and holds its own copies, and the sources we hold don't say whether
Lakeshore itself is "a person engaged in research" or a Certificate recipient. That is why
the decision is organizational and not a statutory finding.

The policy also expects that "[f]or studies in which informed consent is sought," participants are told
the Certificate's protections and limits. Here consent was waived, so nothing attaches to that
expectation.

## What the privacy officer must confirm before EXT-21 runs

This is the finish line for the module: a short list the privacy officer, the IRB's paperwork and
Lakeshore's counsel must be able to tick, with what IT does in each row.

| # | What must be confirmed | Who confirms | Evidence in RSH-0107 | IT's part |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which IRB acted, on what date, for which protocol, and that it covers a contributing blood center's donor data for the current round | Privacy officer, from the hub's paperwork | The IRB approval and waiver documentation, not a paper citation or an email | None, except filing it |
| 2 | That the IRB's consent waiver records the 46.116(f)(3) findings, and that it covers a *recurring* extract | Privacy officer | Waiver findings in the file | Describe the extract accurately to the privacy officer |
| 3 | That Lakeshore's HIPAA basis is its own: limited data set plus data use agreement under 164.514(e) | Privacy officer, with counsel | Written determination | Build and prove the limit |
| 4 | That every EXT-21 field avoids the 164.514(e)(2) list, field by field, including free-text and any "number" that works like a listed identifier | Privacy officer | Reviewed data spec, signed | Remove or reject fields; no free-text fields in v1 |
| 5 | That the data use agreement contains the required terms and names who may use or receive the data | Privacy officer, counsel | Signed agreement | Know which endpoints are authorized |
| 6 | That the coded key is option B (random, stable, crosswalk never leaves Lakeshore) | Privacy officer | Key design note | Generate, protect, back up and inventory the crosswalk |
| 7 | That the Certificate decision is documented | Privacy officer, counsel | Written decision | Execute the controls below |
| 8 | Whether Lakeshore needs its own IRB review or reliance on the program's IRB | Counsel and the hub | **Open: not answered in our sources** | None until decided |

Row 8 is an honest gap. Our Common Rule excerpt does not carry the rules on which institution is
"engaged" in research or how reliance on another IRB is documented. Ask the hub in writing; don't
assume. And for row 1: the *paper* says a single IRB granted the waiver. Documentation from the
actual IRB, for the actual round, is what gets filed.

### Why the privacy officer chose a limited data set and a data use agreement

Her reasoning, as she explains it to the group:

- **Dates are needed.** The protocol studies timing, and the limited data set allows dates.
- **No direct identifier is needed.** The study needs to follow donors over time, not to know who
  they are. A coded key does that, and the crosswalk stays at Lakeshore.
- **It is Lakeshore's own basis.** The program's single-IRB waiver is the program's pathway. If
  Lakeshore relied only on that, a defect in the hub's paperwork would become a defect in
  Lakeshore's disclosure. The data use agreement is a document Lakeshore holds, with terms
  Lakeshore negotiated.
- **The waiver pathway is open but not chosen.** If the hub supplies documentation of an IRB's HIPAA
  authorization waiver with the 164.512(i)(2) contents, that would be a second basis. She doesn't
  need it.

She adds the warning that matters most to IT: "A coded data set is not automatically
de-identified. I'm not going to argue that EXT-21 is de-identified. I'm saying it's a limited data
set, and that has written terms."

### The Certificate decision, in her words and counsel's

Counsel is careful. "I can't tell you the statute puts every Lakeshore copy under a Certificate. The
text we have is written for researchers and award recipients, and Lakeshore's exact status turns on
facts and an agreement we haven't seen. What I can tell you is that the downside of treating it as
covered is some operational friction, and the downside of treating it as *not* covered, if we're
wrong, is handing over research data we couldn't legally hand over."

The decision recorded for RSH-0107, as an organizational decision, is:

> Lakeshore will treat EXT-21 output and the donor-key crosswalk as **information covered by a
> Certificate of Confidentiality**, grounded in 42 U.S.C. 241(d) and NIH's policy NOT-OD-17-109,
> without a claim that the statute settles Lakeshore's exact status. In practice: no disclosure
> outside the research purpose; legal requests routed to counsel; copies tracked; protection
> treated as indefinite.

## What a Certificate means for IT

Each line below is a control or a habit. None of it comes from a regulation's text about IT. It is
the operational consequence of the decision above, and each item is labeled as Lakeshore policy.

1. **Inventory every copy.** The statute says "all copies thereof." List every location that holds
   EXT-21 output rows or the crosswalk: the EXT-21 job's output folder, the staging area before
   release, the QC reconciliation reports that contain rows, **backups** (including offsite and
   long-retention sets), **test and validation copies**, logs that capture row-level content, and
   any dashboard-feedback screenshots saved from the DCC. Register each as a CMDB item with the
   determination that classifies it. A copy you can't find is a copy you can't protect.
2. **Route any subpoena or legal request touching research data to counsel.** That includes court
   orders, subpoenas, agency requests and legislative requests, and also an ordinary-sounding
   request such as "send us everything we have about donor X." The service desk, the systems
   administrator and you do not decide whether the exceptions apply. Counsel does. A one-page
   service desk knowledge article should say: do not respond, do not search, tell counsel the same
   day, and preserve whatever counsel tells you to preserve. A legal hold is separate: preservation
   is not disclosure.
3. **Never use research data for operations.** EXT-21 output and the crosswalk are not a
   convenient second source for operational questions. Don't use them to fix a BECS record, to look
   up a donor, to answer a hospital, for marketing or for donor recontact. If someone has a good
   reason, it goes to the privacy officer and counsel first. The limited data set is lawful only
   for "research, public health, or health care operations" (164.514(e)(3)(i)), but the *agreement*
   narrows the purpose further, and the Certificate narrows it again.
4. **Retention and destruction follow the data use agreement.** The regulation's text doesn't
   require terms on keeping or destroying data, so Lakeshore's agreement must say it. Protection
   being "for perpetuity" does not mean you keep everything forever. It means a copy that still
   exists is still protected, and that destroying a copy needs a record. Destruction has to cover
   backups and test copies, to be documented and to be cleared with counsel if any hold is in
   place.
5. **Log access.** Who read the crosswalk, who touched an output file before release, who released
   it and when it was transferred. This supports Lakeshore's HIPAA obligations (a limited data set
   is PHI), the data use agreement's reporting terms and the ability to answer "who had it?" years
   later. Module 5 turns this into specific controls.
6. **Plan for end of life.** Retiring EXT-21 or refreshing storage should trigger "where did its
   data go?" with a recorded answer.
7. **Keep the ability to stop.** Because of 164.514(e)(4)(iii), Lakeshore may have to discontinue
   disclosure. A transfer that can be paused cleanly, with a log of what went before, is part of
   the design.

## See it in one picture

The diagram shows the three layers in this scenario. The solid arrows are the path Lakeshore chose;
the dotted arrow is the HIPAA pathway it did not choose.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["Hub invitation: RSH-0107, EXT-21"] --> B["Layer 1: Common Rule<br/>single-IRB consent waiver (program's pathway)<br/>documentation filed in RSH-0107"]
    A --> C{"Layer 2: Lakeshore's own HIPAA basis"}
    C -->|"chosen"| D["Limited data set + data use agreement<br/>164.514(e)"]
    C -.->|"not chosen: needs IRB or privacy board<br/>documentation of authorization waiver"| E["164.512(i)"]
    D --> F["Coded donor key, option B<br/>crosswalk stays at Lakeshore"]
    B --> G{"Layer 3: Certificate of Confidentiality"}
    F --> G
    G --> H["Organizational decision:<br/>treat EXT-21 output + crosswalk as covered"]
    H --> I["IT controls: copy inventory, legal requests to counsel,<br/>no operational use, retention per DUA, access logging"]
    I --> J["Privacy officer's written determination<br/>clears RSH-0107 condition 1"]
```

sensitive information" means, and the laws behind them. FDA issues Certificates for research it
regulates, while NIH's policy covers NIH-funded research like REDS, so treat the video as background
on the shared statute, not as the rules for this program. It isn't about blood centers or Lakeshore.

## What an inspector or auditor would look for

For research data, the people asking are a hub's site reviewer, an IRB, an internal auditor, or a
HIPAA reviewer. FDA's interest is the BECS records, not the extract. They would want:

- **The privacy officer's written determination** naming the pathway (limited data set plus data
  use agreement), the date and the reasoning. Bad answer: "Legal said it's fine."
- **The signed data use agreement** with the 164.514(e)(4) terms and the named recipients. Bad
  answer: "It's in the hub's contract somewhere."
- **The IRB documentation**, from the IRB. Bad answer: "The paper says so."
- **A field-by-field review** of the data specification against the 164.514(e)(2) list. Bad
  answer: "We removed names."
- **The copy inventory, legal-request procedure and access logs.** Bad answer: "We'd have to go
  looking."

## Common traps

1. **"The IRB waived consent, so HIPAA is handled."** The consent waiver is a Common Rule finding
   (46.116(f)(3)). HIPAA's authorization is separate, and the covered entity needs *its own* basis:
   documentation of an authorization waiver under 164.512(i), or a limited data set and agreement
   under 164.514(e). Lakeshore chose the latter.
2. **"We took the names out, so it's de-identified."** A limited data set is still PHI
   (164.514(e)(2) defines it as "protected health information that excludes" the listed items).
   A coded set is not automatically de-identified, and the Certificate's definition includes
   information with "at least a very small risk" of identification.
3. **"A Certificate protects us from FDA."** The statute speaks of information "created or compiled
   for purposes of the research," and NIH's own list of permitted disclosures includes ones
   "[r]equired by Federal, State, or local laws (e.g., as required by the Federal Food, Drug, and
   Cosmetic Act [...])," except in legal proceedings. Don't tell Quality anything about FDA access
   that counsel hasn't confirmed. The working assumption is that nothing here changes what FDA may
   see in BECS.
4. **"A Certificate means we can ignore a subpoena."** It means nobody in IT decides. Counsel
   decides, and quickly.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask for the paper, not the summary.** Before EXT-21 touches real data, the file holds the IRB
  documentation, the privacy officer's written determination and the signed agreement. A
  forwarded email isn't any of them.
- **Give the privacy officer a field-by-field data spec.** One row per field, a purpose, and
  whether it could match a 164.514(e)(2) category. Raise free-text fields yourself. Strip them in
  v1 rather than hoping they're clean.
- **Own the copy inventory.** It's an IT deliverable, kept in the CMDB, reviewed at each change to
  EXT-21 and whenever backup or storage changes.
- **Write the legal-request runbook.** One page: who to call, what not to do, what to preserve.
- **Say "organizational decision" every time.** To the CIO, Quality and an auditor, describe the
  Certificate status as Lakeshore's documented decision, grounded in statute and NIH policy. Don't
  say "the law says our data is protected."
- **Escalate scope changes.** A new field, recipient or study, or any operational use of the
  crosswalk, goes to the privacy officer and counsel first.

## The Director's decision for RSH-0107

You record this under the privacy officer's written determination:

> **RSH-0107 condition 1 (privacy and IRB pathway) is cleared when the following are in the file.
> Transfers remain not approved until condition 3 (data agreement and security terms) is also met.**
>
> 1. The program's single-IRB waiver documentation, from the IRB, filed as the program's
>    human-subjects pathway. This is not Lakeshore's HIPAA basis.
> 2. Lakeshore's HIPAA basis is a **limited data set under a data use agreement** (164.514(e)),
>    with a field-by-field review of the data spec and a signed agreement naming recipients.
> 3. The coded donor key is **option B**: random, stable, with the crosswalk never leaving Lakeshore.
> 4. Lakeshore treats EXT-21 output and the crosswalk as **covered by a Certificate of
>    Confidentiality**, as a documented organizational decision. Legal requests go to counsel,
>    copies are inventoried in the CMDB, research data is never used for operations, retention and
>    destruction follow the agreement, and access is logged.
>
> Open: whether Lakeshore relies on the program's IRB through a written reliance arrangement.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: The medical director says the single IRB's consent waiver covers HIPAA. What do you answer?

The waiver is a Common Rule finding under 46.116(f)(3). HIPAA is a separate question: the
covered entity needs its own basis for disclosing PHI, either documentation of an authorization
waiver under 164.512(i) or a limited data set and data use agreement under 164.514(e). The paper
describes a waiver of *informed consent*; it doesn't say a HIPAA authorization waiver exists. This
is a "different rule, different owner" answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Name three things a data use agreement for a limited data set must establish, and one thing it is not required to say.

Any three of: the permitted uses and disclosures; who may use or receive the data; that the
recipient won't use or further disclose it beyond the agreement or the law; that it will use
appropriate safeguards; that it will report unauthorized uses or disclosures; that agents are bound
to the same restrictions; that it won't identify the information or contact individuals
(164.514(e)(4)(ii)). The text lists no required terms on retention or destruction, so those are
Lakeshore's to negotiate. That is a "the regulation is silent" answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Why isn't a limited data set the same as de-identified data?

Because 164.514(e)(2) defines a limited data set as protected health information that excludes
listed direct identifiers. It is still PHI, dates and town or city, State and zip code can remain,
and HIPAA still applies. This course's local sources don't include HIPAA's separate
de-identification text, so we don't apply it. We only note that a coded data set isn't
automatically de-identified.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q4: A subpoena arrives at the service desk naming a donor and "all research data." Walk through what happens.

The service desk doesn't search, answer or release anything. It escalates to counsel the same day.
Counsel decides how the Certificate decision and the exceptions apply and what must be preserved.
IT supplies the copy inventory so counsel knows where data lives, and preserves what counsel
directs. Note that under 42 U.S.C. 241(d)(1)(D) the disclosure bar applies in "any Federal, State,
or local civil, criminal, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding," with consent as the
only exception named there. Lakeshore's status is an organizational decision, so counsel confirms
the approach.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q5: Does the Certificate prevent FDA from inspecting BECS records?

We don't say it does. The statute protects "identifiable, sensitive information" that was "created
or compiled for purposes of the research," and NIH's policy lists disclosures "[r]equired by Federal,
State, or local laws (e.g., as required by the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act [...])" among the
permitted ones, other than in legal proceedings. BECS records exist for blood operations and FDA
recordkeeping. Counsel confirms; the working assumption is that FDA's access to BECS is unchanged.
This is a "do not overstate" answer.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q6: Explain to your CIO in two sentences what the Certificate decision means for IT.

"We've decided, on counsel's advice, to handle the research extract and its donor-code table as
legally protected research data, so IT has to know where every copy lives, send any legal request
to counsel instead of answering it, and never reuse that data for operations. The protection has no
expiry date, so we plan the data's whole lifecycle, backups and retirement included."
:::
